prompt: Why is trans-2-butene more stable than cis-2-butene?

choices.text: The cis isomer has steric strain between its two methyls on the same side
The trans isomer has more substituents on its double bond
choices.why: Both isomers are disubstituted; each double-bond carbon has one methyl.

choices.text: The trans isomer has a stronger π bond between its carbons
choices.why: The difference comes from steric strain between the methyl groups in the cis isomer, not from the π bond.

choices.text: The trans isomer has more hyperconjugation from its methyls
choices.why: Both isomers carry the same two methyl groups on the double bond. The difference the book gives is steric strain in the cis isomer.

explanation: Cis alkenes are less stable than their trans isomers because of steric strain between the two larger substituents on the same side of the double bond. It is the same kind of steric interference seen in the axial conformation of methylcyclohexane.

prompt: From equilibrium measurements, by how much is trans-2-butene more stable than cis-2-butene at room temperature, in kJ/mol?
explanation: Equilibrating the two isomers with a strong acid catalyst shows that the trans isomer is more stable by 2.8 kJ/mol (0.66 kcal/mol) at room temperature, corresponding to a 76 : 24 ratio.

prompt: When cis- and trans-2-butene reach equilibrium at room temperature, what percentage of the mixture is the trans isomer?
explanation: The equilibrium ratio is 76 : 24, trans to cis, reflecting the 2.8 kJ/mol greater stability of trans-2-butene.

prompt: How can cis-2-butene and trans-2-butene be made to interconvert so their equilibrium can be measured?

choices.text: By treating the alkene with a strong acid catalyst
By treating it with H2 and a palladium catalyst
choices.why: That hydrogenates both isomers to butane rather than interconverting them.

choices.text: No treatment is needed, because they interconvert on their own at room temperature
choices.why: Cis–trans interconversion doesn't occur spontaneously.

choices.text: By cooling the mixture well below room temperature
choices.why: Cooling doesn't interconvert them. The book uses a strong acid catalyst.

explanation: Cis–trans interconversion of alkene isomers doesn't occur spontaneously, but it can often be made to happen by treating the alkene with a strong acid catalyst. Letting the isomers reach equilibrium shows which is more stable.

prompt: What do alkenes give when treated with H2 gas in the presence of a palladium or platinum catalyst?

choices.text: The corresponding alkane
The more stable cis–trans isomer
choices.why: Hydrogenation adds H2 across the double bond; both cis- and trans-2-butene give butane.

choices.text: An alkyl halide
choices.why: No halogen is present. Adding H2 gives an alkane.

choices.text: An alcohol
choices.why: No oxygen is present. Adding H2 gives an alkane.

explanation: Alkenes undergo a hydrogenation reaction to give the corresponding alkane when treated with H2 gas and a catalyst such as palladium or platinum. Both cis- and trans-2-butene give butane.

prompt: What is ΔH°_hydrog for trans-2-butene, in kJ/mol, including its sign?
explanation: Table 7.6.1 gives ΔH°_hydrog = −115 kJ/mol (−27.4 kcal/mol) for trans-2-butene and −119 kJ/mol (−28.3 kcal/mol) for cis-2-butene.

prompt: From their heats of hydrogenation, by how much is trans-2-butene more stable than cis-2-butene, in kJ/mol?
explanation: cis-2-Butene has ΔH°_hydrog = −119 kJ/mol and trans-2-butene −115 kJ/mol. The cis isomer releases 4 kJ/mol more heat, so trans is more stable by 4 kJ/mol.

prompt: Why is more energy released when cis-2-butene is hydrogenated than when trans-2-butene is?

choices.text: The cis isomer starts higher in energy, and both give butane
The cis isomer gives a less stable alkane than the trans isomer
choices.why: Both isomers give the same alkane, butane, so the products are at the same energy level.

choices.text: The cis isomer reacts faster with hydrogen on the catalyst
choices.why: How fast a reaction goes doesn't set how much energy it releases. The difference lies in the starting energies.

choices.text: The cis isomer forms stronger C–H bonds in its product
choices.why: Both isomers give the same product, butane, with the same bonds. The cis isomer simply has more energy to begin with.

explanation: Because cis-2-butene is less stable, it starts at a higher energy level. After reaction both are at the same level (butane), so more energy is released by the cis isomer (Figure 7.6.1).

prompt: Heats of hydrogenation give a 4 kJ/mol energy difference between the 2-butene isomers, but equilibrium data give 2.8 kJ/mol. Which reason does the book give for the difference?

choices.text: Heats of reaction measure ΔH°, while equilibrium constants measure ΔG°
Equilibrium constants measure ΔH°, while heats of reaction measure ΔG°
choices.why: It's the other way around: heats of reaction give ΔH° and equilibrium constants give ΔG°.

choices.text: The two methods were applied to different isomers of 2-butene
choices.why: Both methods compare the same cis and trans isomers.

choices.text: Hydrogenating the two isomers gives two different alkanes
choices.why: Both isomers give butane.

explanation: The values agree reasonably well but aren't identical for two reasons. Heats of hydrogenation are difficult to measure accurately, so there is probably some experimental error, and heats of reaction measure ΔH° while equilibrium constants measure ΔG°.

prompt: What is ΔH°_hydrog for ethylene, H2C=CH2, in kJ/mol, including its sign?
explanation: Ethylene has ΔH°_hydrog = −136 kJ/mol (−32.6 kcal/mol), the largest heat release in Table 7.6.1. It has no substituents on its double bond.

prompt: Which alkene in Table 7.6.1 is the most stable?

choices.text: (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2
H2C=CH2
choices.why: Ethylene releases the most heat on hydrogenation (−136 kJ/mol), so it's the least stable.

choices.text: (CH3)2C=CHCH3
choices.why: This trisubstituted alkene (−112 kJ/mol) is quite stable, but the tetrasubstituted one releases even less heat (−110 kJ/mol).

choices.text: CH3CH=CH2
choices.why: Monosubstituted propene (−125 kJ/mol) is near the bottom of the stability order.

explanation: The less heat an alkene releases on hydrogenation, the more stable it is. Tetrasubstituted (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2 has the smallest value, −110 kJ/mol, so it is the most stable.

prompt: What is the stability order of alkenes, most stable first?

choices.text: Tetrasubstituted > trisubstituted > disubstituted > monosubstituted
Monosubstituted > disubstituted > trisubstituted > tetrasubstituted
choices.why: That's reversed. Alkenes become more stable with increasing substitution.

choices.text: Trisubstituted > tetrasubstituted > disubstituted > monosubstituted
choices.why: Tetrasubstituted (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2 releases less heat (−110 kJ/mol) than trisubstituted (CH3)2C=CHCH3 (−112 kJ/mol), so it is more stable.

choices.text: Disubstituted > monosubstituted > trisubstituted > tetrasubstituted
choices.why: Stability increases steadily with the number of substituents on the double bond.

explanation: Table 7.6.1 shows that alkenes become more stable with increasing substitution: tetrasubstituted > trisubstituted > disubstituted > monosubstituted.

prompt: Using Table 7.6.1, how many kJ/mol more heat is released when propene, CH3CH=CH2, is hydrogenated than when (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2 is?
explanation: Propene has ΔH°_hydrog = −125 kJ/mol and (CH3)2C=C(CH3)2 has −110 kJ/mol. The 15 kJ/mol difference reflects how much more stable the tetrasubstituted alkene is than the monosubstituted one.

prompt: What is hyperconjugation in an alkene?

choices.text: A stabilizing interaction between the C=C π orbital and adjacent C–H σ bonds on substituents
A destabilizing crowding between two substituents on the same side of the double bond
choices.why: That's steric strain, the reason cis alkenes are less stable. Hyperconjugation is stabilizing.

choices.text: The sideways overlap of two p orbitals that forms the π bond
choices.why: That's the π bond itself. Hyperconjugation is an extra interaction between the π orbital and neighboring C–H σ bonds.

choices.text: A stabilizing interaction between the C=C π orbital and C–H bonds on the double-bond carbons themselves
choices.why: The C–H σ bonds involved are on the substituents attached to the double bond, as in the C=C–C–H grouping.

explanation: Hyperconjugation is a stabilizing interaction between the C=C π orbital and adjacent C–H σ bonds on substituents. The more substituents on the double bond, the more hyperconjugation occurs and the more stable the alkene.

prompt: In the molecular orbital description of hyperconjugation in an alkene, over how many atoms does the stabilizing bonding MO extend?
explanation: There is a bonding MO that extends over the four-atom C=C–C–H grouping (Figure 7.6.2): the two double-bond carbons, the substituent carbon, and one of its hydrogens.

prompt: Besides hyperconjugation, what second factor makes more highly substituted alkenes more stable?

choices.text: They have more sp3–sp2 bonds, which are somewhat stronger than sp3–sp3 bonds
They have more sp3–sp3 bonds, which are stronger than sp3–sp2 bonds
choices.why: It's the other way around: a bond between an sp2 and an sp3 carbon is somewhat stronger than one between two sp3 carbons.

choices.text: Their substituents are all on the same side of the double bond
choices.why: Substituents on the same side cause steric strain, which is destabilizing.

choices.text: They have more hydrogens on the double-bond carbons
choices.why: More highly substituted alkenes have fewer hydrogens on the double-bond carbons, not more.

explanation: A bond between an sp2 carbon and an sp3 carbon is somewhat stronger than a bond between two sp3 carbons. More highly substituted alkenes always have a higher ratio of sp3–sp2 to sp3–sp3 bonds, so they are more stable.

prompt: How many sp3–sp2 carbon–carbon single bonds does 2-butene, CH3CH=CHCH3, have?
explanation: Each methyl carbon (sp3) is bonded to a double-bond carbon (sp2), giving two sp3–sp2 bonds. 1-Butene, CH2=CHCH2CH3, has one sp3–sp2 bond and one sp3–sp3 bond, which helps explain why 2-butene is more stable.

prompt: Which is more stable: 1-butene, CH2=CHCH2CH3, or 2-methylpropene, (CH3)2C=CH2?

choices.text: 2-Methylpropene, because its double bond is disubstituted
1-Butene, because its chain is unbranched
choices.why: Branching isn't the criterion. 1-Butene's double bond carries only one substituent, so it is less stable.

choices.text: They are equally stable, because both are C4H8
choices.why: Isomers with the same formula can differ in stability. The number of substituents on the double bond decides here.

choices.text: 1-Butene, because its double bond is at the end of the chain
choices.why: Its end-of-chain double bond carries only one substituent, which makes it less stable than a disubstituted one.

explanation: 1-Butene is monosubstituted and 2-methylpropene is disubstituted. Since alkenes become more stable with increasing substitution, 2-methylpropene is more stable (Exercise 7.6.1).

prompt: Which is more stable: 1-methylcyclohexene or 3-methylcyclohexene?

choices.text: 1-Methylcyclohexene, whose double bond is trisubstituted
3-Methylcyclohexene, whose methyl is away from the double bond
choices.why: Moving the methyl off the double bond lowers substitution from three to two, which makes the alkene less stable.

choices.text: Neither, since both have exactly one methyl group
choices.why: Where the methyl sits matters: on a double-bond carbon it adds to the substitution of the double bond.

choices.text: 3-Methylcyclohexene, whose double bond has more hydrogens
choices.why: More hydrogens on the double bond means fewer substituents, which means less stability.

explanation: In 1-methylcyclohexene, the double bond carries the methyl group and two ring carbons (trisubstituted). In 3-methylcyclohexene, it carries only two ring carbons (disubstituted). More substituted alkenes are more stable (Exercise 7.6.1).

prompt: Which is more stable: cis-2-hexene or trans-2-hexene?

choices.text: trans-2-Hexene
cis-2-Hexene
choices.why: In the cis isomer, the two alkyl groups are on the same side and crowd each other (steric strain).

choices.text: They are equally stable, because both are disubstituted
choices.why: Both are disubstituted, but the cis isomer suffers steric strain between the groups on the same side.

choices.text: It can't be decided without heats of hydrogenation for 2-hexene
choices.why: The general rule settles it: cis alkenes are less stable than their trans isomers because of steric strain.

explanation: As with 2-butene, the trans isomer is more stable because the cis isomer has steric strain between the two alkyl groups on the same side of the double bond (Exercise 7.6.1).
